bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Expansion project execution and approval timing — Timely execution of ongoing expansion projects remains important to achieving the Company's planned growth objectives, and any delay in implementation may postpone the expected operational and financial benefits. This is the binding constraint across a pipeline that includes the 600 MW to 1,200 MW Binjkot expansion, 141 MW of hydro under development, four coal blocks and the pellet doubling — environmental clearance, forest clearance and mining plan approvals determine project schedules more than construction capability does, equipment suppliers in India are heavily booked, and the 50 MW captive solar plant has already slipped on transmission right-of-way issues.
- Coal mining project development risk — statutory approvals, land acquisition and supporting infrastructure — The successful development of the Company's coal mining projects requires timely statutory approvals and land acquisition, efficient project execution and adequate supporting infrastructure. Surface rights, transportation corridors and railway sidings frequently sit on the critical path, requiring sustained engagement well ahead of first production. Since the plan to quadruple mining capacity towards 7.10 MTPA underpins both fuel security and the new commercial coal business, slippage here propagates into the power business.
- Commodity price volatility across steel, ferro alloys, pellets and electricity — Volatility in steel, ferro alloys, pellets and electricity prices may affect profitability during periods of market weakness, and global overcapacity together with lower-priced imports may continue to influence domestic steel prices and export competitiveness. Steel realisations stayed below the previous year for most of FY 2025-26 before recovering late in the year, and merchant exchange power prices moved between ` 3.33 and ` 4.30 per unit across quarters, so earnings for spot-reliant generation move with weather, fuel and grid demand rather than own performance.
- Raw material availability and input cost exposure, including imported coking coal and manganese/chrome ore — International price movements in high grade coal, manganese ore and other critical raw materials may affect cost structures. Import reliance for coking coal, together with freight and energy cost movement, remains a structural consideration, and access to quality manganese and chrome ore directly determines ferro alloy operating margin — which is why the Company is still searching for long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration.
- Operational consistency, equipment reliability and plant availability — Maintaining consistent operational performance across manufacturing facilities, power plants and mining operations remains important for sustaining productivity, cost efficiency and customer commitments, with continued focus on equipment reliability, plant availability and preventive maintenance to minimise disruptions. The planned shutdown of one 30 MW captive power unit from December 2025 for turbine replacement demonstrably bore on steel and ferro alloy production during the year, and utilisation already varies widely by line (sponge iron 96% against wire rods 64%).
- Regulatory, policy and environmental compliance across mining, power and taxation — Changes in government policies relating to mining, power, taxation, environmental regulations and international trade may influence the business environment, and compliance with statutory, environmental and regulatory requirements remains an ongoing priority across all businesses and project locations. Increasing environmental standards, carbon-related regulations and sustainability expectations may require higher investment in cleaner technologies and compliance — a live exposure for a coal-fired, coal-mining group.
- Evolution of India's power market and rising renewable penetration — The gradual evolution of India's power market, including increasing renewable penetration and changing procurement patterns, may influence the operating environment for conventional power generators. Energy contributes approximately two-thirds of consolidated EBITDA, so the terms on which thermal capacity is contracted and dispatched matter disproportionately; grid and storage constraints raise the value of dispatchable generation but also the need for matching transmission and storage investment.
- Climate and hydrological variability affecting mining, logistics and hydropower — Climate-related events, including irregular rainfall and extreme weather conditions, may affect mining activity, logistics and hydropower generation. The hydro fleet's FY 2025-26 plant load factors were materially below the thermal asset's — Gullu 58.81%, Loharkhet 48.60%, Rongnichu 44% and Rehar 38.58% against 79% at the Binjkot IPP — and the Company is expanding hydro from 166.7 MW towards approximately 309 MW, increasing exposure to hydrology.
- Availability of skilled manpower and specialised technical expertise — Availability of skilled manpower and specialised technical expertise remains important for supporting existing operations as well as future expansion projects — a constraint that scales with a pipeline spanning thermal, hydro, solar, four coal blocks and a pellet doubling across multiple states.
- Cybersecurity and IT/digital infrastructure continuity — Information technology systems, digital infrastructure and cybersecurity continue to receive management attention to ensure business continuity and protect operational data. The Company runs SAP and other integrated systems across finance, procurement, production, inventory, sales and human resources, so an availability or integrity failure would reach core operating processes.

business.body: SEML operates three closely connected businesses: power generation (thermal, hydro and solar assets), mining (commercial coal blocks and captive iron ore) and manufacturing that converts those resources into iron ore pellets, sponge iron, billets, wire rods, H.B. wire and ferro alloys. Iron ore from its own mine becomes pellets, pellets become sponge iron, sponge iron becomes billets, and billets become wire rods and wire, with power supplied from its own plants at every stage. Pellets go mainly to nearby sponge iron plants, sponge iron/billets/wire rods/HB wire to small and medium downstream companies in the vicinity, ferro alloys chiefly to large steel mills domestically and via export, and power mainly to state distribution utilities.

outlook.body:
- Transform from a metals company into an Energy-plus-Minerals enterprise — energy already contributes roughly two-thirds of consolidated earnings, mining is becoming a business in its own right, and metals is the beneficiary of both.
- Double the Binjkot thermal power plant's capacity to 1,200 MW through a brownfield 2 x 300 MW to 4 x 300 MW expansion at the existing site, where land, water, grid connectivity, coal handling and railway siding are already in place.
- Enhance hydropower generation capacity to more than 300 MW, taking hydro from the present 166.7 MW to approximately 309 MW through three Chhattisgarh projects totalling 74 MW and a 66 MW project in Arunachal Pradesh.
- Quadruple mining capacity through the development of the Shahpur West, Gare Palma IV/5, Bartunga and Senduri coal blocks, moving approved capacity towards 7.10 MTPA and turning mining from a support function into a commercial business with a market alongside the captive one.
- More than double Raipur pellet capacity to 20 lakh tonnes per annum, timed against iron ore mines expected to open in Chhattisgarh over the next two to three years.
- Deepen vertical integration so that market exposures become controlled inputs — coal from own mines feeding own power, own power feeding furnaces, own ore feeding pellets — with roughly 35% of pellets, 85% of sponge iron and 85% of billets consumed internally.
- Size capital expenditure to match internal cash generation, sequence projects so each new investment begins contributing to earnings before the next major commitment is made, and evaluate every rupee deployed against long-term earnings resilience rather than short-term optics.
- Continue to evaluate opportunities in emerging areas such as coal gasification, deepen digital and process capabilities across operations, and remain alert to selective, well-evaluated opportunities that strengthen the value proposition.
- Secure long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration into the ferro alloy business, where raw material and power together determine competitiveness.
- Extend the value-added end of the product range — Low-Phosphorus Silico Manganese and 6 mm ribbed TMT in coil form were introduced during the year for specific customer requirements.
- Shift the energy mix toward cleaner sources through the 166.7 MW hydropower portfolio and the upcoming captive solar project, structuring sustainability into how capacity is planned and capital allocated rather than running it as a separate initiative.
- Prioritise consistency of growth across many years over fastest growth in any single year, ensuring scale and control grow together rather than at each other's expense.
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: SEML's capital expenditure programme is focused on expanding operating capacity, strengthening resource security and increasing value addition, funded by internal cash generation. In POWER, the largest investment is the proposed brownfield expansion of the Binjkot independent power plant from 2 x 300 MW to 4 x 300 MW, taking site capacity to 1,200 MW; land for the additional units is already held, water availability is established, grid connectivity is in place, and the coal handling facilities and railway siding built for the operating units can support the expanded plant, which is expected to shorten execution and improve capital efficiency relative to a greenfield project — environmental clearance is under process and capital deployment is expected to gather pace after statutory approvals. Four hydropower projects totalling 141 MW are under development: three in Chhattisgarh with a combined 74 MW, and a 66 MW project at Rahung village on the Gang River in Arunachal Pradesh (Khuitam) where the Company has acquired a majority stake in the project company through wholly owned subsidiary Sarda Renewable Energy Limited, expected to be commissioned within five years; together these take hydro capacity from the present 166.7 MW to approximately 309 MW. A 24.9 MW Kotaiveera small hydro project on the IB river in Chhattisgarh is in the final stage of approvals with work expected to start during the current financial year. A 50 MW captive solar plant is under implementation at Kharora to reduce reliance on grid power at the manufacturing complex; commissioning has been delayed by right-of-way issues on the transmission line, with an alternate 33 KV evacuation route being laid, and the plant is now expected before the end of Q3 FY 2026-27 (by October 2026). One 30 MW captive power unit was shut down from 1 December 2025 for replacement with a new energy-efficient BHEL turbine and generator, due to start operation in August 2026. In MINING, four coal blocks are advancing alongside the operating Gare Palma IV/7, taking approved capacity towards 7.10 MTPA: Shahpur West (explosive magazine constructed, PESO licence received, production expected before the end of the current financial year, and it will substitute imported high grade coal fully); Gare Palma IV/5 (physical possession taken July 2025, CMPDIL geological report approved, mining plan and mine closure plan cleared by the Ministry of Coal, forest land diversion under process, proposed for conversion from underground working to a 2.0 MTPA opencast operation, with 57 months from 04.02.2025 to start); Bartunga Hill (a JV led by the Company with a 67% share on a revenue-sharing basis with SECL, mining plan approved for an annual peak rated capacity of 2.1 MnT, terms of reference for environmental clearance secured, EIA studies nearing completion, production hoped before the end of next financial year); and Senduri in Madhya Pradesh (declared successful bidder, development agreement executed, DGPS survey completed, a 67-borehole exploration plan approved, detailed exploration ongoing). Gare Palma IV/7's approved capacity was raised during the year from 1.68 MTPA to 1.80 MTPA and production reached that ceiling exactly; a dedicated railway siding is under development to reduce evacuation cost. JV company Natural Resources Energy Private Limited was declared successful bidder for the Surjagarh-1 iron ore block in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra, with the prospecting/composite licence executed, forest permission for core drilling received and exploration and survey work commenced. In METALS, the Board approved raising pellet capacity at Raipur from 0.9 to 2.0 million tonnes with environmental clearance already in place, timed against iron ore mines expected to open in Chhattisgarh over the next two to three years. A mineral wool project was successfully installed and commissioned during the year as a waste-management initiative, and the Rock Mineral Wool Plant at subsidiary SMAL stabilised its operations. Twelve diesel loaders, five trailers and one forklift were replaced with electric vehicles. The Company also continues to evaluate coal gasification and to search for long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration in ferro alloys.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- India's steel industry is expected to maintain healthy growth over the medium term, supported by expanding infrastructure investment, increasing urbanisation, rising manufacturing activity and favourable government policies; India remains one of the few large economies with a strong and diversified demand outlook.
- Domestic finished steel consumption is expected to grow steadily, supported by infrastructure development, housing, transportation, renewable energy and capital goods manufacturing, with programmes such as Make in India, the National Manufacturing Mission and PLI schemes strengthening demand across defence, railways, engineering, shipbuilding and renewable energy equipment.
- Industry steel capacity is projected to increase towards 235-240 MTPA, while the National Steel Policy target of 300 MTPA by 2030-31 continues to guide investments across the sector; per capita finished steel consumption crossed 100 kg for the first time against a policy target of 160 kg by 2030-31.
- Ferro alloy domestic demand could continue growing at approximately 7% to 8% annually over the medium term, supported by higher steel production, infrastructure development, manufacturing expansion and rising consumption of value-added steel products; manganese alloys benefit from domestic demand while ferro chrome remains linked to global stainless-steel markets and export conditions.
- ICRA projects Indian electricity demand to grow at a CAGR of 6.0% to 6.5% between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, with electric vehicles, green hydrogen and data centres contributing 20% to 25% of incremental demand; peak demand is expected to rise from 256 GW in FY 2025-26 to around 335 GW by FY 2029-30.
- The Government of India has revised its thermal power roadmap to add 97 GW of coal-based capacity by FY 2034-35, taking total thermal capacity to around 307 GW — thermal remains essential for baseload and dispatchable power, providing a favourable operating environment for SEML's IPP.
- Rising electricity demand across India is expected to improve capacity utilisation across the Company's thermal and hydropower assets.
- Competitiveness in ferro alloys is determined by operational efficiency, secure access to raw materials, competitive energy costs and consistent product quality — electricity is among the largest cost components, making the 80 MW captive power plant at Visakhapatnam a structural advantage.
- Mining competitiveness is shifting from volume to coal quality, evacuation efficiency and grade matching; the sector is becoming a market rather than a supply chain, and the Company's beneficiation capacity and captive consumption position it for that shift.
- Premium-grade iron ore and pellet imports roughly doubled nationally as steelmakers became more specific about grade, blending and plant-level requirements, widening pellet use in efficient iron making.
- Steel prices improved during the fourth quarter of FY 2025-26, although average realisations for the full year remained below the previous year's levels.
- Expansion of India's steel industry is expected to support sustained demand for pellets, sponge iron, ferro alloys and value-added steel products.
- Global electricity demand is expected to grow at an average annual rate of around 3.6% between 2026 and 2030 to about 33,600 TWh, reinforcing long-term opportunities across SEML's diversified thermal, hydro and solar portfolio.
- Iron ore production in India rose to 305 MT from about 289 million tonnes, with output expected to reach 340 to 345 million tonnes in FY 2026-27 — the backdrop against which the pellet expansion is timed.

risks.note: Timely execution of ongoing expansion projects remains important to achieving the Company's planned growth objectives, and any delay in implementation may postpone the expected operational and financial benefits. This is the binding constraint across a pipeline that includes the 600 MW to 1,200 MW Binjkot expansion, 141 MW of hydro under development, four coal blocks and the pellet doubling — environmental clearance, forest clearance and mining plan approvals determine project schedules more than construction capability does, equipment suppliers in India are heavily booked, and the 50 MW captive solar plant has already slipped on transmission right-of-way issues.
risks.risk: Expansion project execution and approval timing

risks.note: The successful development of the Company's coal mining projects requires timely statutory approvals and land acquisition, efficient project execution and adequate supporting infrastructure. Surface rights, transportation corridors and railway sidings frequently sit on the critical path, requiring sustained engagement well ahead of first production. Since the plan to quadruple mining capacity towards 7.10 MTPA underpins both fuel security and the new commercial coal business, slippage here propagates into the power business.
risks.risk: Coal mining project development risk — statutory approvals, land acquisition and supporting infrastructure

risks.note: Volatility in steel, ferro alloys, pellets and electricity prices may affect profitability during periods of market weakness, and global overcapacity together with lower-priced imports may continue to influence domestic steel prices and export competitiveness. Steel realisations stayed below the previous year for most of FY 2025-26 before recovering late in the year, and merchant exchange power prices moved between ` 3.33 and ` 4.30 per unit across quarters, so earnings for spot-reliant generation move with weather, fuel and grid demand rather than own performance.
risks.risk: Commodity price volatility across steel, ferro alloys, pellets and electricity

risks.note: International price movements in high grade coal, manganese ore and other critical raw materials may affect cost structures. Import reliance for coking coal, together with freight and energy cost movement, remains a structural consideration, and access to quality manganese and chrome ore directly determines ferro alloy operating margin — which is why the Company is still searching for long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration.
risks.risk: Raw material availability and input cost exposure, including imported coking coal and manganese/chrome ore

risks.note: Maintaining consistent operational performance across manufacturing facilities, power plants and mining operations remains important for sustaining productivity, cost efficiency and customer commitments, with continued focus on equipment reliability, plant availability and preventive maintenance to minimise disruptions. The planned shutdown of one 30 MW captive power unit from December 2025 for turbine replacement demonstrably bore on steel and ferro alloy production during the year, and utilisation already varies widely by line (sponge iron 96% against wire rods 64%).
risks.risk: Operational consistency, equipment reliability and plant availability

risks.note: Changes in government policies relating to mining, power, taxation, environmental regulations and international trade may influence the business environment, and compliance with statutory, environmental and regulatory requirements remains an ongoing priority across all businesses and project locations. Increasing environmental standards, carbon-related regulations and sustainability expectations may require higher investment in cleaner technologies and compliance — a live exposure for a coal-fired, coal-mining group.
risks.risk: Regulatory, policy and environmental compliance across mining, power and taxation

risks.note: The gradual evolution of India's power market, including increasing renewable penetration and changing procurement patterns, may influence the operating environment for conventional power generators. Energy contributes approximately two-thirds of consolidated EBITDA, so the terms on which thermal capacity is contracted and dispatched matter disproportionately; grid and storage constraints raise the value of dispatchable generation but also the need for matching transmission and storage investment.
risks.risk: Evolution of India's power market and rising renewable penetration

currentContext.expansion: SEML's capital expenditure programme is focused on expanding operating capacity, strengthening resource security and increasing value addition, funded by internal cash generation. In POWER, the largest investment is the proposed brownfield expansion of the Binjkot independent power plant from 2 x 300 MW to 4 x 300 MW, taking site capacity to 1,200 MW; land for the additional units is already held, water availability is established, grid connectivity is in place, and the coal handling facilities and railway siding built for the operating units can support the expanded plant, which is expected to shorten execution and improve capital efficiency relative to a greenfield project — environmental clearance is under process and capital deployment is expected to gather pace after statutory approvals. Four hydropower projects totalling 141 MW are under development: three in Chhattisgarh with a combined 74 MW, and a 66 MW project at Rahung village on the Gang River in Arunachal Pradesh (Khuitam) where the Company has acquired a majority stake in the project company through wholly owned subsidiary Sarda Renewable Energy Limited, expected to be commissioned within five years; together these take hydro capacity from the present 166.7 MW to approximately 309 MW. A 24.9 MW Kotaiveera small hydro project on the IB river in Chhattisgarh is in the final stage of approvals with work expected to start during the current financial year. A 50 MW captive solar plant is under implementation at Kharora to reduce reliance on grid power at the manufacturing complex; commissioning has been delayed by right-of-way issues on the transmission line, with an alternate 33 KV evacuation route being laid, and the plant is now expected before the end of Q3 FY 2026-27 (by October 2026). One 30 MW captive power unit was shut down from 1 December 2025 for replacement with a new energy-efficient BHEL turbine and generator, due to start operation in August 2026. In MINING, four coal blocks are advancing alongside the operating Gare Palma IV/7, taking approved capacity towards 7.10 MTPA: Shahpur West (explosive magazine constructed, PESO licence received, production expected before the end of the current financial year, and it will substitute imported high grade coal fully); Gare Palma IV/5 (physical possession taken July 2025, CMPDIL geological report approved, mining plan and mine closure plan cleared by the Ministry of Coal, forest land diversion under process, proposed for conversion from underground working to a 2.0 MTPA opencast operation, with 57 months from 04.02.2025 to start); Bartunga Hill (a JV led by the Company with a 67% share on a revenue-sharing basis with SECL, mining plan approved for an annual peak rated capacity of 2.1 MnT, terms of reference for environmental clearance secured, EIA studies nearing completion, production hoped before the end of next financial year); and Senduri in Madhya Pradesh (declared successful bidder, development agreement executed, DGPS survey completed, a 67-borehole exploration plan approved, detailed exploration ongoing). Gare Palma IV/7's approved capacity was raised during the year from 1.68 MTPA to 1.80 MTPA and production reached that ceiling exactly; a dedicated railway siding is under development to reduce evacuation cost. JV company Natural Resources Energy Private Limited was declared successful bidder for the Surjagarh-1 iron ore block in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra, with the prospecting/composite licence executed, forest permission for core drilling received and exploration and survey work commenced. In METALS, the Board approved raising pellet capacity at Raipur from 0.9 to 2.0 million tonnes with environmental clearance already in place, timed against iron ore mines expected to open in Chhattisgarh over the next two to three years. A mineral wool project was successfully installed and commissioned during the year as a waste-management initiative, and the Rock Mineral Wool Plant at subsidiary SMAL stabilised its operations. Twelve diesel loaders, five trailers and one forklift were replaced with electric vehicles. The Company also continues to evaluate coal gasification and to search for long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration in ferro alloys.
currentContext.mdna: India's steel industry is expected to maintain healthy growth over the medium term, supported by expanding infrastructure investment, increasing urbanisation, rising manufacturing activity and favourable government policies; India remains one of the few large economies with a strong and diversified demand outlook.|Domestic finished steel consumption is expected to grow steadily, supported by infrastructure development, housing, transportation, renewable energy and capital goods manufacturing, with programmes such as Make in India, the National Manufacturing Mission and PLI schemes strengthening demand across defence, railways, engineering, shipbuilding and renewable energy equipment.|Industry steel capacity is projected to increase towards 235-240 MTPA, while the National Steel Policy target of 300 MTPA by 2030-31 continues to guide investments across the sector; per capita finished steel consumption crossed 100 kg for the first time against a policy target of 160 kg by 2030-31.|Ferro alloy domestic demand could continue growing at approximately 7% to 8% annually over the medium term, supported by higher steel production, infrastructure development, manufacturing expansion and rising consumption of value-added steel products; manganese alloys benefit from domestic demand while ferro chrome remains linked to global stainless-steel markets and export conditions.|ICRA projects Indian electricity demand to grow at a CAGR of 6.0% to 6.5% between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, with electric vehicles, green hydrogen and data centres contributing 20% to 25% of incremental demand; peak demand is expected to rise from 256 GW in FY 2025-26 to around 335 GW by FY 2029-30.|The Government of India has revised its thermal power roadmap to add 97 GW of coal-based capacity by FY 2034-35, taking total thermal capacity to around 307 GW — thermal remains essential for baseload and dispatchable power, providing a favourable operating environment for SEML's IPP.|Rising electricity demand across India is expected to improve capacity utilisation across the Company's thermal and hydropower assets.|Competitiveness in ferro alloys is determined by operational efficiency, secure access to raw materials, competitive energy costs and consistent product quality — electricity is among the largest cost components, making the 80 MW captive power plant at Visakhapatnam a structural advantage.|Mining competitiveness is shifting from volume to coal quality, evacuation efficiency and grade matching; the sector is becoming a market rather than a supply chain, and the Company's beneficiation capacity and captive consumption position it for that shift.|Premium-grade iron ore and pellet imports roughly doubled nationally as steelmakers became more specific about grade, blending and plant-level requirements, widening pellet use in efficient iron making.|Steel prices improved during the fourth quarter of FY 2025-26, although average realisations for the full year remained below the previous year's levels.|Expansion of India's steel industry is expected to support sustained demand for pellets, sponge iron, ferro alloys and value-added steel products.|Global electricity demand is expected to grow at an average annual rate of around 3.6% between 2026 and 2030 to about 33,600 TWh, reinforcing long-term opportunities across SEML's diversified thermal, hydro and solar portfolio.|Iron ore production in India rose to 305 MT from about 289 million tonnes, with output expected to reach 340 to 345 million tonnes in FY 2026-27 — the backdrop against which the pellet expansion is timed.

risks.risk: Expansion project execution and approval timing
risks.note: Timely execution of ongoing expansion projects remains important to achieving the Company's planned growth objectives, and any delay in implementation may postpone the expected operational and financial benefits. This is the binding constraint across a pipeline that includes the 600 MW to 1,200 MW Binjkot expansion, 141 MW of hydro under development, four coal blocks and the pellet doubling — environmental clearance, forest clearance and mining plan approvals determine project schedules more than construction capability does, equipment suppliers in India are heavily booked, and the 50 MW captive solar plant has already slipped on transmission right-of-way issues.

risks.risk: Coal mining project development risk — statutory approvals, land acquisition and supporting infrastructure
risks.note: The successful development of the Company's coal mining projects requires timely statutory approvals and land acquisition, efficient project execution and adequate supporting infrastructure. Surface rights, transportation corridors and railway sidings frequently sit on the critical path, requiring sustained engagement well ahead of first production. Since the plan to quadruple mining capacity towards 7.10 MTPA underpins both fuel security and the new commercial coal business, slippage here propagates into the power business.

risks.risk: Commodity price volatility across steel, ferro alloys, pellets and electricity
risks.note: Volatility in steel, ferro alloys, pellets and electricity prices may affect profitability during periods of market weakness, and global overcapacity together with lower-priced imports may continue to influence domestic steel prices and export competitiveness. Steel realisations stayed below the previous year for most of FY 2025-26 before recovering late in the year, and merchant exchange power prices moved between ` 3.33 and ` 4.30 per unit across quarters, so earnings for spot-reliant generation move with weather, fuel and grid demand rather than own performance.

risks.risk: Raw material availability and input cost exposure, including imported coking coal and manganese/chrome ore
risks.note: International price movements in high grade coal, manganese ore and other critical raw materials may affect cost structures. Import reliance for coking coal, together with freight and energy cost movement, remains a structural consideration, and access to quality manganese and chrome ore directly determines ferro alloy operating margin — which is why the Company is still searching for long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration.

risks.risk: Operational consistency, equipment reliability and plant availability
risks.note: Maintaining consistent operational performance across manufacturing facilities, power plants and mining operations remains important for sustaining productivity, cost efficiency and customer commitments, with continued focus on equipment reliability, plant availability and preventive maintenance to minimise disruptions. The planned shutdown of one 30 MW captive power unit from December 2025 for turbine replacement demonstrably bore on steel and ferro alloy production during the year, and utilisation already varies widely by line (sponge iron 96% against wire rods 64%).

risks.risk: Regulatory, policy and environmental compliance across mining, power and taxation
risks.note: Changes in government policies relating to mining, power, taxation, environmental regulations and international trade may influence the business environment, and compliance with statutory, environmental and regulatory requirements remains an ongoing priority across all businesses and project locations. Increasing environmental standards, carbon-related regulations and sustainability expectations may require higher investment in cleaner technologies and compliance — a live exposure for a coal-fired, coal-mining group.

risks.risk: Evolution of India's power market and rising renewable penetration
risks.note: The gradual evolution of India's power market, including increasing renewable penetration and changing procurement patterns, may influence the operating environment for conventional power generators. Energy contributes approximately two-thirds of consolidated EBITDA, so the terms on which thermal capacity is contracted and dispatched matter disproportionately; grid and storage constraints raise the value of dispatchable generation but also the need for matching transmission and storage investment.

risks.risk: Climate and hydrological variability affecting mining, logistics and hydropower
risks.note: Climate-related events, including irregular rainfall and extreme weather conditions, may affect mining activity, logistics and hydropower generation. The hydro fleet's FY 2025-26 plant load factors were materially below the thermal asset's — Gullu 58.81%, Loharkhet 48.60%, Rongnichu 44% and Rehar 38.58% against 79% at the Binjkot IPP — and the Company is expanding hydro from 166.7 MW towards approximately 309 MW, increasing exposure to hydrology.

risks.risk: Availability of skilled manpower and specialised technical expertise
risks.note: Availability of skilled manpower and specialised technical expertise remains important for supporting existing operations as well as future expansion projects — a constraint that scales with a pipeline spanning thermal, hydro, solar, four coal blocks and a pellet doubling across multiple states.

Information technology systems, digital infrastructure and cybersecurity continue to receive management attention to ensure business continuity and protect operational data. The Company runs SAP and other integrated systems across finance, procurement, production, inventory, sales and human resources, so an availability or integrity failure would reach core operating processes.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Sarda Energy & Minerals Limited (SEML) is a vertically integrated Chhattisgarh-based energy, mining and metals group that has evolved over five decades from a pure-play steel manufacturer into a diversified enterprise where energy contributes roughly two-thirds of consolidated earnings.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: SEML operates three closely connected businesses: power generation (thermal, hydro and solar assets), mining (commercial coal blocks and captive iron ore) and manufacturing that converts those resources into iron ore pellets, sponge iron, billets, wire rods, H.B. wire and ferro alloys. Iron ore from its own mine becomes pellets, pellets become sponge iron, sponge iron becomes billets, and billets become wire rods and wire, with power supplied from its own plants at every stage. Pellets go mainly to nearby sponge iron plants, sponge iron/billets/wire rods/HB wire to small and medium downstream companies in the vicinity, ferro alloys chiefly to large steel mills domestically and via export, and power mainly to state distribution utilities.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India's steel industry is expected to maintain healthy growth over the medium term, supported by expanding infrastructure investment, increasing urbanisation, rising manufacturing activity and favourable government policies; India remains one of the few large economies with a strong and diversified demand outlook.
- Domestic finished steel consumption is expected to grow steadily, supported by infrastructure development, housing, transportation, renewable energy and capital goods manufacturing, with programmes such as Make in India, the National Manufacturing Mission and PLI schemes strengthening demand across defence, railways, engineering, shipbuilding and renewable energy equipment.
- Industry steel capacity is projected to increase towards 235-240 MTPA, while the National Steel Policy target of 300 MTPA by 2030-31 continues to guide investments across the sector; per capita finished steel consumption crossed 100 kg for the first time against a policy target of 160 kg by 2030-31.
- Ferro alloy domestic demand could continue growing at approximately 7% to 8% annually over the medium term, supported by higher steel production, infrastructure development, manufacturing expansion and rising consumption of value-added steel products; manganese alloys benefit from domestic demand while ferro chrome remains linked to global stainless-steel markets and export conditions.
- ICRA projects Indian electricity demand to grow at a CAGR of 6.0% to 6.5% between FY 2026-27 and FY 2030-31, with electric vehicles, green hydrogen and data centres contributing 20% to 25% of incremental demand; peak demand is expected to rise from 256 GW in FY 2025-26 to around 335 GW by FY 2029-30.
- The Government of India has revised its thermal power roadmap to add 97 GW of coal-based capacity by FY 2034-35, taking total thermal capacity to around 307 GW — thermal remains essential for baseload and dispatchable power, providing a favourable operating environment for SEML's IPP.
- Rising electricity demand across India is expected to improve capacity utilisation across the Company's thermal and hydropower assets.
- Competitiveness in ferro alloys is determined by operational efficiency, secure access to raw materials, competitive energy costs and consistent product quality — electricity is among the largest cost components, making the 80 MW captive power plant at Visakhapatnam a structural advantage.
- Mining competitiveness is shifting from volume to coal quality, evacuation efficiency and grade matching; the sector is becoming a market rather than a supply chain, and the Company's beneficiation capacity and captive consumption position it for that shift.
- Premium-grade iron ore and pellet imports roughly doubled nationally as steelmakers became more specific about grade, blending and plant-level requirements, widening pellet use in efficient iron making.
- Steel prices improved during the fourth quarter of FY 2025-26, although average realisations for the full year remained below the previous year's levels.
- Expansion of India's steel industry is expected to support sustained demand for pellets, sponge iron, ferro alloys and value-added steel products.
- Global electricity demand is expected to grow at an average annual rate of around 3.6% between 2026 and 2030 to about 33,600 TWh, reinforcing long-term opportunities across SEML's diversified thermal, hydro and solar portfolio.
- Iron ore production in India rose to 305 MT from about 289 million tonnes, with output expected to reach 340 to 345 million tonnes in FY 2026-27 — the backdrop against which the pellet expansion is timed.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: SEML's capital expenditure programme is focused on expanding operating capacity, strengthening resource security and increasing value addition, funded by internal cash generation. In POWER, the largest investment is the proposed brownfield expansion of the Binjkot independent power plant from 2 x 300 MW to 4 x 300 MW, taking site capacity to 1,200 MW; land for the additional units is already held, water availability is established, grid connectivity is in place, and the coal handling facilities and railway siding built for the operating units can support the expanded plant, which is expected to shorten execution and improve capital efficiency relative to a greenfield project — environmental clearance is under process and capital deployment is expected to gather pace after statutory approvals. Four hydropower projects totalling 141 MW are under development: three in Chhattisgarh with a combined 74 MW, and a 66 MW project at Rahung village on the Gang River in Arunachal Pradesh (Khuitam) where the Company has acquired a majority stake in the project company through wholly owned subsidiary Sarda Renewable Energy Limited, expected to be commissioned within five years; together these take hydro capacity from the present 166.7 MW to approximately 309 MW. A 24.9 MW Kotaiveera small hydro project on the IB river in Chhattisgarh is in the final stage of approvals with work expected to start during the current financial year. A 50 MW captive solar plant is under implementation at Kharora to reduce reliance on grid power at the manufacturing complex; commissioning has been delayed by right-of-way issues on the transmission line, with an alternate 33 KV evacuation route being laid, and the plant is now expected before the end of Q3 FY 2026-27 (by October 2026). One 30 MW captive power unit was shut down from 1 December 2025 for replacement with a new energy-efficient BHEL turbine and generator, due to start operation in August 2026. In MINING, four coal blocks are advancing alongside the operating Gare Palma IV/7, taking approved capacity towards 7.10 MTPA: Shahpur West (explosive magazine constructed, PESO licence received, production expected before the end of the current financial year, and it will substitute imported high grade coal fully); Gare Palma IV/5 (physical possession taken July 2025, CMPDIL geological report approved, mining plan and mine closure plan cleared by the Ministry of Coal, forest land diversion under process, proposed for conversion from underground working to a 2.0 MTPA opencast operation, with 57 months from 04.02.2025 to start); Bartunga Hill (a JV led by the Company with a 67% share on a revenue-sharing basis with SECL, mining plan approved for an annual peak rated capacity of 2.1 MnT, terms of reference for environmental clearance secured, EIA studies nearing completion, production hoped before the end of next financial year); and Senduri in Madhya Pradesh (declared successful bidder, development agreement executed, DGPS survey completed, a 67-borehole exploration plan approved, detailed exploration ongoing). Gare Palma IV/7's approved capacity was raised during the year from 1.68 MTPA to 1.80 MTPA and production reached that ceiling exactly; a dedicated railway siding is under development to reduce evacuation cost. JV company Natural Resources Energy Private Limited was declared successful bidder for the Surjagarh-1 iron ore block in Gadchiroli, Maharashtra, with the prospecting/composite licence executed, forest permission for core drilling received and exploration and survey work commenced. In METALS, the Board approved raising pellet capacity at Raipur from 0.9 to 2.0 million tonnes with environmental clearance already in place, timed against iron ore mines expected to open in Chhattisgarh over the next two to three years. A mineral wool project was successfully installed and commissioned during the year as a waste-management initiative, and the Rock Mineral Wool Plant at subsidiary SMAL stabilised its operations. Twelve diesel loaders, five trailers and one forklift were replaced with electric vehicles. The Company also continues to evaluate coal gasification and to search for long-term manganese resources to extend backward integration in ferro alloys.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body: Confident and transformational; Emphasizes shift from cyclical commodity player to stable energy-mining integrated model. Prudent on steel cycle (believes bottomed out but wary of global war impact). Aggressive on capacity doubling with strong balance sheet support.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Vertical integration across mining, power generation and downstream metals — a power plant that owns its coal is insulated from index movements competitors must absorb, a furnace that owns its power is insulated from tariff movements, and a pellet plant that owns its ore is insulated from grade shortages others must buy through
- Captive power across the chain: captive thermal at Siltara and Visakhapatnam plus 21.5 MW of waste heat recovery and the hydro portfolio reduce exposure to purchased power — electricity is among the largest cost components in ferro alloy production, making captive generation a structural rather than incidental advantage
- Captive coal from Gare Palma IV/7 sited next to the thermal plant, with 14,65,781 tonnes consumed captively during the year and an integrated 1.80 MTPA washery improving grade before use
- Internal offtake reduces spot-price exposure at each stage — around 35% of pellets, 85% of sponge iron and 85% of billets are consumed internally
- Diversified portfolio across power, mining and metals in four states, delivering 6,122 million kWh during the year with energy contributing approximately two-thirds of consolidated EBITDA
- Contracted revenue visibility in power: medium and long-term power purchase agreements covering a growing share of thermal capacity, and forty- and thirty-five-year agreements on hydro assets
- Brownfield expansion optionality at Binjkot — land, water availability, grid connectivity, coal handling facilities and railway siding already in place, expected to shorten execution timelines and improve capital efficiency
- Strong credit standing: long-term rating of AA- (Positive) and short-term rating of A1+ from CRISIL, reflecting a sound financial profile and prudent capital management
- Two-Star Export House recognition supporting international market access in ferro alloys
- Promoter and promoter group holding 73.16% of the total paid-up equity share capital, and a Board whose skills chart covers iron & steel, mining, power and strategic planning

hero.oneLiner: Sarda Energy & Minerals Limited (SEML) is a vertically integrated Chhattisgarh-based energy, mining and metals group that has evolved over five decades from a pure-play steel manufacturer into a diversified enterprise where energy contributes roughly two-thirds of consolidated earnings.
